Certainly it's something Spencer that you and I talked about a lot. President Hearst, Blake Hearst, has made this a cornerstone of his efforts leading Farm Bureau to be sure that we get connected. The digital divide became bigger during the pandemic than it has ever been before with virtual learning and school is closed. And your kid can keep up with the virtual classes because they have that connectedness of high speed broadband. It's still tough, but it's unbelievably tough. It's impossibly tough if they're not connected. And then you combine that with the health issue you know, not only as you mentioned in the case of members of your family, just not having to make the effort to get to the doctor or if you can't get the doctor, you miss the appointment and the doctor's time is also impacted and it's much more easily managed. And then as I've said a number of times, I think it's really the key to whether many of our small communities in our state thrive or go just eventually no longer economically viable. One of the things we've seen in the pandemic is people beginning to think, well, if I can work from home, why can't I live wherever I want to live? And there are lots of people who would like to look at that 1500 or 1000 person or 500 person or even 200 person community in our state where church activities don't matter and school sports don't matter and people may not know every kid's name but they actually do know every house every kid lives in and that's a very appealing lifestyle to lots of people today people that have great jobs with great income with many of many people like that but they can't make that choice if that community is not connected in a way that allows them to have the kind of income that they'd like to have. And so I think it's really the lifeblood of our communities and communities that get connected are going to, I think, really grow in the next five and 10 years because of what we've just gone through.
